title: A deep look at the strange galaxy Centaurus A
caption: The galaxy Centaurus A (NGC 5128), imaged by the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope at La Silla, Chile
celestial: NGC 5128 · constellation Centaurus · about 12 million light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: Ranked #13 on ESO’s published “Top 100 Images” list (an institutional selection, not an audience score).

story: This deep portrait shows the peculiar galaxy Centaurus A, also cataloged as NGC 5128, about 12 million light-years away in the constellation Centaurus. It was made with the Wide Field Imager, a camera mounted on the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope at ESO's La Silla Observatory in Chile.

The picture's depth comes from patience. Its exposures add up to more than 50 hours in total, which makes it probably the deepest view ever created of this unusual and spectacular object. Long exposures build up faint light that a short snapshot would miss, and that is how the dimmer outer parts of a galaxy can be traced.

Centaurus A is classed as an elliptical galaxy with an active nucleus. An active galactic nucleus is a compact galaxy center that gives off far more energy than its stars alone would explain. Several of the filters used isolate the light of glowing oxygen and hydrogen gas.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (33.87 x 33.12 arcminutes) and distance (12 million light years), the frame spans roughly 118,000 × 116,000 light-years. Its light set out about 12 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: The Wide Field Imager on the MPG/ESO 2.2-meter telescope recorded visible light through several filters, including ones for oxygen and hydrogen-alpha emission. The color mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: More than 50 hours of accumulated exposure gather far more light than the eye can, revealing faint structure no visual observer could see.
